readingInstruction: Read Daniel 3:1-4:37. Three men are thrown into a furnace for refusing to bow, and a fourth appears with them. Then Nebuchadnezzar, the proudest man on earth, is humbled and learns that Heaven rules. Read the three men’s reply in 3:16-18 carefully.
settingTheScene: Chapter 3 happens some years after the dream of chapter 2. Nebuchadnezzar builds a gold statue ninety feet high and commands everyone to bow when the music plays. Three of Daniel’s friends, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, refuse. Chapter 4 is a first-person account from the king himself, a testimony of how God humbled him for his pride, then restored him.
observation: “If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king” (3:17).
“But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up” (3:18).
“Behold, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods” (3:25).
“Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants” (3:28).
“The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (4:17).
“Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?” (4:30).
“At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me” (4:34).
“And those who walk in pride he is able to humble” (4:37).
interpretation:
The three men’s reply to the king is among the greatest declarations of faith in the Bible. They do not argue or beg. They say that God is able to deliver them. And they add: “But if not.” Their obedience does not depend on a miracle. They will not bow whether or not God rescues them. This is faith that is not tied to outcome. It trusts God’s character, not his results.

The furnace is heated seven times hotter. It is so hot that it kills the soldiers who throw them in. But inside, there are four men walking, unbound, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods. The rescue shows that God is present in the fire. He does not always spare us from the furnace, but he is with us in it. When they come out, they do not even smell of smoke. The king blesses their God and decrees that no one may speak against him.

Chapter 4 is the king’s personal story. He has a dream of a great tree that is cut down, and Daniel tells him that the tree is himself. For seven periods of time, he will be driven from among men and live like an animal, until he acknowledges that Heaven rules. Daniel gives pastoral advice: “Break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.” A year later, while walking on his roof, the king boasts of Babylon, “which I have built by my mighty power.” The words are still in his mouth when judgment falls.

When his sanity returns, he lifts his eyes to heaven and blesses the Most High. His testimony ends with a statement of the book’s theme: “All his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.” The greatest emperor of the age is brought to confess what Daniel’s friends knew all along.
connection: Isaiah 43:2 says, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you… when you walk through fire you shall not be burned.” Hebrews 11:34 mentions those who “quenched the power of fire.” Acts 5:29: “We must obey God rather than men.” Revelation 13:15 shows a similar demand to worship an image. Matthew 1:23: Immanuel, God with us. Proverbs 16:18 says pride goes before destruction. 1 Peter 5:5-6 says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
application:
Pray “But if not” for a situation where you do not know how God will act. Commit to obedience regardless of the outcome.

Take comfort that Jesus is with you in your furnace.

Examine your own “Is not this great Babylon?” boast. Where might God be humbling pride in you?
prayerPrompts: Tell God what fire you are facing.
Say, “Even if he does not,” and tell him whom you will serve.
Thank him that he walks with you in the fire.
